docs.title: Opsflow Documentation
docs.text:
Opsflow helps operations teams orchestrate workflows across cloud environments. Use this site to find onboarding steps, daily runbooks, and API references.

  • Read Getting Started to set up environments.
  • Visit the Operations section for runbooks.
  • Check the Reference pages when integrating with the Opsflow API.

Need help? Open a ticket in the Opsflow Support Portal or reach out in #opsflow-docs on Slack.

docs.title: Appendix
docs.text:
title: Appendix: limits, references, and checklists summary: Collects quota checks, required ports, operational checklists, and reference links.

This appendix centralizes recurring implementation details for quick use during planning and support.

docs.title: Includes
docs.text:
• Quota and capacity checklist.
  • Connectivity and port expectations.
  • Pre-deployment and post-deployment validation checklist.

docs.title: Architecture and deployment models
docs.text: The managed deployment includes Elasticsearch data and ingest paths, Kibana for visualization and administration, and supporting Azure networking and storage resources.

docs.title: Deployment models
docs.text:
• Public deployment: endpoints are reachable over public DNS with restricted access policies.
  • Private deployment: endpoints are reachable only through private networking and approved routes.

docs.title: Security boundaries
docs.text: Platform resources are isolated in managed Azure resource groups. Access is controlled through least-privilege roles, network boundaries, and audited administrative actions.

docs.title: Deploying Opsflw managed Elastic Stack
docs.text: Deployments follow a controlled provisioning workflow with environment inputs validated before resource creation.

docs.title: Deployment flow
docs.text:
1. Start a deployment request for the target environment.
  2. Provide approved network, identity, and retention parameters.
  3. Monitor deployment status until health checks pass.

docs.title: Completion criteria
docs.text: A deployment is complete when endpoint checks, cluster health, and baseline policy validations are successful.

docs.title: DNS and endpoint access
docs.text: Endpoint access depends on correct DNS records and expected certificate resolution for each environment.

docs.title: DNS scenarios
docs.text:
• Public DNS for internet-reachable deployments.
  • Private DNS zones for internal-only deployments.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Verify name resolution, TLS certificate trust, and endpoint reachability before handover to application teams.

docs.title: Elastic license management
docs.text: Opsflw Connect operates the Elastic Stack under a commercial subscription to unlock advanced security and observability features. Proper license management keeps the cluster compliant and avoids service interruptions.

docs.title: License model
docs.text:
• The deployment uses the Elastic Enterprise license tier to access machine learning jobs, Alerting, and Spaces.
  • Usage is measured in resource-metric units (RMUs) across data nodes, ingest capacity, and machine learning workloads.
  • License files are stored securely in the Opsflw secrets manager and rotated before expiration.

docs.title: Renewal process
docs.text:
1. Track license expiration dates in the central renewal calendar at least 90 days out.
  2. Request updated license files from Elastic with projected growth estimates.
  3. Validate the new license in staging using elastic-license install --scope staging and monitor for warnings.
  4. Schedule production installation during a maintenance window and confirm the cluster reports the renewed expiration.

Document the renewal in the change log and attach the confirmation email for audit readiness.

docs.title: Compliance monitoring
docs.text:
• Enable license usage alerts in Kibana to notify the platform team when consumption approaches 80% of the limit.
  • Review monthly RMU reports to ensure tenant workloads align with contracted capacity.
  • Coordinate with finance and procurement during quarterly business reviews to adjust entitlements proactively.

Rely on the Opsflw Connect profiles to enforce consistent access controls after each license update.

docs.title: Introduction to Opsflw managed Elastic Stack on Azure
docs.text: Opsflw managed Elastic Stack on Azure provides a supported observability platform for logs, metrics, and traces. This guide is written for end users who need to onboard workloads, access Kibana and Elasticsearch, and operate safely within platform guardrails.

docs.title: What this guide covers
docs.text:
• How the managed service is deployed and accessed.
  • What prerequisites your Azure and network teams must satisfy.
  • How to operate, troubleshoot, and request support.

docs.title: Shared responsibility
docs.text: Opsflw operates the managed control plane, platform upgrades, and baseline security controls. Your team manages tenant onboarding, access governance, and data retention choices aligned with your policies.

docs.title: License and feature management
docs.text: Elastic license status determines feature availability and operational limits.

docs.title: What to manage
docs.text:
• License validity and renewal windows.
  • Feature access controlled by environment policy.
  • Capacity trends that can affect licensed limits.

For current renewal workflow details, refer to Elastic license management.

docs.title: Network design prerequisites
docs.text: Network design should be finalized before provisioning to avoid rework and connectivity issues.

docs.title: Baseline requirements
docs.text:
• Non-overlapping CIDR ranges for platform and tenant networks.
  • Defined DNS authority for public and private endpoints.
  • Approved outbound routing path and firewall policy alignment.

Coordinate with central network teams for peering, transit, and on-premises integration requirements.

docs.title: Operations and lifecycle management
docs.text: Day-two operations should follow approved maintenance and change windows.

docs.title: Operational areas
docs.text:
• Scaling and performance tuning.
  • Scheduled maintenance and platform upgrades.
  • Backup, restore, and disaster recovery readiness.

Track operational actions with audit-ready change records.

docs.title: Elastic Stack deployment overview
docs.text: Opsflw Connect ships a managed Elastic Stack cluster to centralize logs, metrics, and traces from every connected environment. The deployment follows a repeatable architecture so day-two operations stay predictable.

docs.title: Cluster layout
docs.text:
• Ingest nodes scale horizontally to accept Beats, Elastic Agent, and API traffic.
  • Data nodes store time-series indices with lifecycle policies tuned for 30-day hot, 90-day warm retention.
  • Master nodes anchor cluster coordination and receive upgrades first during maintenance windows.

All nodes run inside hardened subnets with security groups allowing limited inbound ports. Outbound traffic routes through shared NAT gateways controlled by the network overview policies.

docs.title: Deployment automation
docs.text:
The Elastic deployment is provisioned through Terraform modules managed in the Opsflw IaC repository. Pipelines ensure each change:

  1. Validates the plan against staging.
  2. Executes in production during an approved maintenance window.
  3. Verifies cluster health and index lifecycle status before closing the change.

docs.title: Integration points
docs.text:
• Control plane services ship audit logs through Beats shippers.
  • Tenant workloads forward telemetry using fleet-managed Elastic Agents.
  • Runbooks rely on Kibana dashboards for incident response and compliance reporting.

Continue with the profiles overview to understand how teams tailor Elastic access and dashboards per tenant.

docs.title: Post-deployment network configuration
docs.text: After provisioning, configure required connectivity so users and workloads can reach Elastic endpoints.

docs.title: Common post-deployment tasks
docs.text:
• Configure VNet peering or approved transit model.
  • Update route tables for tenant and shared services traffic.
  • Validate egress behavior through approved security controls.

Document all route and peering changes in your change management system.

docs.title: Prerequisites and planning
docs.text: Before deployment, validate subscription ownership, target region, and service quotas with your Azure administrators.

docs.title: Required checks
docs.text:
• Confirm required Azure resource providers are registered.
  • Confirm quota capacity for compute, networking, and storage.
  • Confirm naming, tagging, and policy requirements for your organization.

docs.title: Planning outputs
docs.text: Capture environment names, region choices, expected ingestion volume, and retention targets before provisioning.

docs.title: Elastic profiles overview
docs.text: Elastic profiles extend the Opsflw Connect profile system to observability data. They map tenant requirements to index lifecycle policies, role mappings, and curated dashboards so teams can grant least-privilege access quickly.

docs.title: What profiles configure
docs.text:
• Data views specify index patterns, default time ranges, and filters for dashboards.
  • Role mappings align tenant SSO groups with Elastic roles that control read and write permissions.
  • Lifecycle policies enforce retention and rollover schedules that match compliance obligations.

Each profile references a baseline set of Kibana objects stored in Git, ensuring reproducible dashboards across environments.

docs.title: Workflow for updates
docs.text:
1. Clone the Elastic content repository and create a feature branch for the profile change.
  2. Update the JSON exports or Fleet packages that define dashboards and visualizations.
  3. Submit a pull request with screenshots, retention impact, and expected migration steps.

Automation syncs merged changes into staging first, then production during the next maintenance window.

docs.title: Validation checklist
docs.text:
• Confirm role mappings continue to enforce least privilege with automated access tests.
  • Verify dashboards load within SLO targets after the sync completes.
  • Ensure lifecycle policies keep storage costs within the allocated budget by reviewing hot and warm usage.

docs.title: Accessing Kibana and Elasticsearch securely
docs.text: Use identity federation and role-based access control to enforce least privilege.

docs.title: Access steps
docs.text:
1. Validate identity provider integration for your tenant.
  2. Assign approved roles for Kibana and Elasticsearch use cases.
  3. Confirm access with a non-admin test account.

Avoid shared administrator accounts and rotate secrets according to policy.

docs.title: Troubleshooting and support
docs.text: Use a structured approach to reduce time to resolution.

docs.title: First-response checklist
docs.text:
• Validate endpoint and DNS behavior.
  • Confirm role mappings and identity provider status.
  • Review cluster health and ingestion pipeline status.

Escalate with environment details, timestamps, and exact failing operations.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Follow these steps to bring your Opsflow workspace online:

  1. Clone the repo:
git clone https://github.com/opsflow/opsflw-docs.git
cd opsflw-docs
  1. Install dependencies inside a virtual environment:
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
  1. Serve docs locally while editing:
mkdocs serve

When the server is running, browse to http://127.0.0.1:8000 to preview your changes.

docs.title: Backup Playbook
docs.text: Opsflow stores configuration data in the control plane and artifacts in S3-compatible storage.

docs.title: Nightly Backup Routine
docs.text:
1. Trigger the opsflow-backup workflow in the customer portal.
  2. Verify the job status under Operations ▸ Jobs.
  3. Confirm that the artifact landed in the designated bucket.

docs.title: Restore Checklist
docs.text:
• Identify the backup timestamp that matches the incident window.
  • Run the restore job with the backup ID:
opsflowctl restore --backup-id <timestamp>
  • Validate restored pipelines in the staging environment before promoting back to production.

docs.title: Compliance and governance
docs.text: Opsflw Connect operations follow governance and control practices designed for enterprise-managed services.

docs.title: Governance outcomes
docs.text:
End users can expect:

  • Controlled change management for service-impacting actions
  • Traceable support and operations workflows
  • Access governance through role-based controls
  • Security and operational oversight processes

docs.title: Compliance posture
docs.text:
Opsflw Connect is operated to support common enterprise compliance needs, including controlled access, auditability, and standardized operational procedures.

Specific regulatory mappings and implementation artifacts are handled through formal customer and compliance channels.

docs.title: Your role as a customer
docs.text:
To maintain compliance alignment, customer teams should:

  • Assign access by business role
  • Keep user and ownership records current
  • Use formal support and change channels
  • Follow internal governance and data handling policies

docs.title: How to get support and submit tickets
docs.text: Submit all requests and incidents through the Opsflw Customer Support Portal so work can be tracked, prioritized, and escalated correctly.

docs.title: Before opening a ticket
docs.text:
• Confirm whether this is a service request, defect, or incident.
  • Capture affected environment(s), timeframe, and observed behavior.
  • Check active maintenance communications and known incidents.

docs.title: Ticket submission checklist
docs.text:
1. Select severity based on business impact.
  2. Add a clear summary and expected vs actual behavior.
  3. Include reproduction steps if the issue is repeatable.
  4. Attach logs, screenshots, and correlation/request IDs.
  5. State business impact and required recovery timeline.

docs.title: After submission
docs.text:
• Monitor ticket updates in the portal.
  • Respond quickly to triage requests for missing context.
  • Escalate through your assigned support contacts for high-severity events.

For planned work and expected-impact updates, refer to What is a maintenance window.

docs.title: Introduction to Opsflw Connect
docs.text:
Opsflw Connect is the customer portal and operations interface for applications deployed through the Opsflw platform.

It gives customers one place to access deployed services, check operational status, manage access expectations, and request support.

Tip

Opsflw Connect does not run your applications directly. It provides operational access and management for applications deployed through Opsflw.

docs.title: Why Opsflw Connect exists
docs.text:
Opsflw Connect exists to reduce operational overhead for customer teams by standardizing how you interact with managed applications.

With Opsflw Connect, you can:

  • Access deployed applications and service entry points
  • Monitor deployment and service status
  • Follow security and access governance workflows
  • Submit and track support requests
  • Stay informed about maintenance and operational events

docs.title: Who should use this documentation
docs.text:
This section is intended for:

  • Application owners responsible for deployed services
  • DevOps/SRE teams handling day-to-day operations
  • Security teams reviewing access and control practices
  • IT administrators managing user and process governance

docs.title: How it works (high-level)
docs.text:
[User]
  |
  v
[Opsflw Connect Portal]
  |
  v
[Opsflw Control Plane]
  |
  v
[Customer Cloud Infrastructure]
  |
  v
[Deployed Applications]

This model gives users a clear operational interface while Opsflw manages the underlying platform lifecycle.

docs.title: Application access
docs.text:
• Find your managed applications
  • Retrieve approved service access information
  • Navigate to service-specific operations and support guidance

docs.title: Operations monitoring
docs.text:
• View deployment status and service state
  • Track planned maintenance notifications
  • Follow operational updates through standardized channels

docs.title: Security and access control
docs.text:
• Operate within role-based access expectations
  • Follow managed credential and secret-handling policies
  • Align with customer and platform governance requirements

docs.title: Support and maintenance
docs.text:
• Submit incidents and service requests
  • Track ticket progress and responses
  • Understand maintenance window expectations and user actions

docs.title: Typical user workflow
docs.text:
1. Deploy an application through the approved onboarding flow.
  2. Receive access to Opsflw Connect.
  3. Open your application record in the portal.
  4. Check status, access information, and operational guidance.
  5. Submit support tickets when help is required.

docs.title: First steps for new users
docs.text:
1. Review the Azure overview to understand what is managed for you.
  2. Confirm your role and access level.
  3. Review security and password management expectations.
  4. Learn the support ticket workflow.
  5. Review maintenance window guidance before production changes.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text:
• Managed application: A service where Opsflw deploys and operates platform foundations.
  • Control plane: The managed orchestration layer that coordinates platform operations.
  • Access model: The role-based method used to govern user permissions.
  • Deployment instance: A specific customer deployment of an application environment.
  • Maintenance window: A scheduled period for planned service-impacting changes.
  • Support workflow: The formal process for incidents, requests, and escalation.

docs.text: Azure Cloud Overview | Security | Password and secrets | Compliance | Maintenance windows | Support and tickets

docs.title: Maintenance window guidelines
docs.text: Opsflw Connect coordinates maintenance windows across shared platform services so application teams can plan changes with minimal downtime. Follow these guidelines when requesting or executing maintenance work.

docs.title: Scheduling windows
docs.text:
1. Submit a change request with the proposed scope, environments, and fallback plan.
  2. Confirm the window does not overlap with tenant blackouts or critical campaigns.
  3. Reserve a secondary window in case contingency actions require rollback or follow-up tasks.

The change advisory board reviews high-impact requests weekly. Routine patches with pre-approved procedures may use the express path described in the operations runbooks.

docs.title: Communication checklist
docs.text:
• Publish the maintenance details in the status page and #opsflw-notices Slack channel 72 hours ahead.
  • Send targeted emails to impacted tenant contacts with timeline, expected impact, and rollback triggers.
  • Host a live bridge during the window for real-time coordination and incident escalation.

Document outcomes and lessons learned in the change record before closing the request.

docs.title: Execution best practices
docs.text:
• Freeze configuration drift with opsflowctl lock --scope <environment> before work begins.
  • Monitor platform health via the Elastic Stack dashboards and automated synthetic checks.
  • Follow the rollback plan immediately if SLO breaches persist beyond the agreed error budget.

Update the maintenance calendar after completion so future planning remains accurate.

docs.title: Network overview
docs.text: Opsflw Connect uses a split architecture between the control plane and managed Kubernetes environments. End-user workloads run in managed clusters, while Opsflw Connect services coordinate lifecycle operations and deployment updates.

docs.title: High-level connectivity model
docs.text:
• Control-plane services run in cloud-hosted Opsflw platform infrastructure.
  • Opsflw Connect Agent runs in the managed Kubernetes cluster.
  • Secure communication is maintained between agent and control plane.

docs.title: Deployment-time network actions
docs.text:
During deployment and updates, Opsflw automation may perform:

  • Private DNS configuration for managed cluster endpoints.
  • VNet/VPC peering between required platform and managed environments.
  • Secret and parameter propagation through secure cloud-native mechanisms.

These steps are automated through deployment workflows and GitOps sync.

docs.title: End-user considerations
docs.text:
• Keep your network/security team informed of private connectivity requirements.
  • Validate DNS resolution and endpoint reachability after major changes.
  • Report connectivity regressions through the support portal with environment and region details.

docs.title: Opsflw Connect on Azure Cloud
docs.text: Opsflw Connect on Azure Cloud is delivered as a managed application service. From an end-user perspective, Opsflw provisions and operates the core platform foundation so your teams can focus on using the service, not building it.

docs.title: What a managed application means
docs.text:
A managed application means Opsflw is responsible for deploying, operating, and maintaining the platform components required to run the service.

You consume the service through approved access channels and support workflows.

docs.title: What end users get access to
docs.text:
End users and customer administrators receive access to:

  • The managed application experience and service endpoints
  • Operational status and planned maintenance communications
  • Support request and incident reporting channels
  • Role-based access aligned with organizational permissions

docs.title: What Opsflw manages for you
docs.text:
Opsflw deploys and maintains the Azure platform foundation, including:

  • AKS-based runtime environment
  • Required supporting infrastructure for secure and reliable operations
  • Platform updates, lifecycle operations, and service health monitoring

Implementation details are intentionally abstracted from end-user workflows.

docs.title: Opsflw Connect platform overview
docs.text:
Opsflw Connect delivers a modular orchestration layer that all Opsflw applications build on. The platform combines shared data services, automation pipelines, and unified access controls so teams can operate distributed environments with confidence.

  • Understand how the control plane coordinates workflows across cloud regions.
  • Learn which shared services power identity, networking, and observability.
  • Follow links to deeper guides on networking, maintenance windows, and profile management.

docs.title: Platform composition
docs.text:
The platform splits into three primary planes:

  1. Control plane handles API requests, workflow scheduling, and configuration state.
  2. Data plane runs tenant workloads inside isolated clusters, applying policies from the control plane.
  3. Operations plane exposes audit logging, alerting, and backup services for day-two operations.

Each plane is secured with organization-level authentication, role-based authorization, and dedicated network segments described in the network overview.

docs.title: Shared services
docs.text:
Opsflw Connect centralizes the following services so feature teams can focus on application logic:

  • Identity service federates users and service accounts across applications using SAML or OIDC.
  • Networking service provisions VLANs, VPC peering, and firewall policies for workloads.
  • Observability stack ships metrics, logs, and traces into the Elastic Stack deployment.
  • Configuration registry stores tenant and environment metadata that applications consume at runtime.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: Review the rest of the Opsflw Connect platform section to understand the shared guardrails before configuring application-specific features.

docs.title: Password and secrets management
docs.text: Opsflw Connect uses managed secret handling practices for credentials and other sensitive values.

docs.title: KeyVault-based secret storage
docs.text: Sensitive values are stored and protected in Azure Key Vault-based secret management services. Secrets are not intended to be shared through email, chat, or ad-hoc documents.

docs.title: End-user guidance
docs.text:
• Never hardcode passwords or tokens in scripts or tickets
  • Use approved secret workflows for credential requests or rotation
  • Limit credential sharing to authorized users only
  • Report suspected credential exposure immediately through support

docs.title: Rotation and lifecycle
docs.text:
Credential and secret lifecycle activities, including rotation and replacement, are handled through controlled operational processes.

If your team needs credential-related changes, submit a support request with business context and required timeline.

docs.title: Profiles overview
docs.text:
Opsflw Connect deployments use profile-driven configuration to keep provisioning and updates consistent across environments.

In deployment workflows, profile and size selections are part of the parameters used to generate platform values and deployment overlays.

docs.title: What profiles affect
docs.text:
• Baseline application configuration in platform value files
  • Environment-specific overrides in deployment value files
  • Lifecycle changes applied through GitOps synchronization

docs.title: Related configuration sources
docs.text:
Opsflw Connect configuration is assembled from layered sources, including:

  • Base values files
  • Cloud/channel-specific value files
  • Platform values
  • Deployment overlays

This layered model allows platform defaults with controlled per-deployment customization.

docs.title: End-user guidance
docs.text:
1. Choose profile and size carefully at initial deployment.
  2. For scaling or behavior changes, submit an update request with the target profile/size change.
  3. Validate post-update behavior after GitOps synchronization completes.

docs.title: Security overview
docs.text: Opsflw Connect applies a security-first operating model for managed applications on Azure.

docs.title: Security principles
docs.text:
• Least-privilege access for users and service identities
  • Role-based access control for customer and operator responsibilities
  • Controlled operational change through approved workflows
  • Monitoring and response processes for security-relevant events

docs.title: End-user expectations
docs.text:
As an end user, you should expect:

  • Access based on assigned role and approved business need
  • Authentication and authorization controls aligned with enterprise policy
  • Security updates applied through planned platform operations

docs.title: Shared responsibility
docs.text:
Opsflw manages platform and service security controls.

Customers remain responsible for:

  • User governance in their organization
  • Correct use of assigned permissions
  • Internal policy compliance for data and access usage

docs.title: Support emails and contacts
docs.text: Use the Opsflw support process based on urgency and business impact.

docs.title: Primary support channel
docs.text:
• Use the Opsflw Customer Support Portal as the system of record for all requests and incidents.
  • Open one ticket per issue to ensure correct triage, ownership, and SLA tracking.

docs.title: Escalation contacts
docs.text: If your organization has named escalation contacts, use the support contact list provided during onboarding. Keep the portal ticket updated while escalating.

docs.title: Required details in first contact
docs.text:
• Environment or deployment name
  • Region and cloud
  • Impact summary and affected users/services
  • Start time (with timezone) and current status

docs.title: What is a maintenance window
docs.text:
A maintenance window is a scheduled time block when Opsflw performs planned platform or application changes, such as upgrades, configuration updates, and security patching.

Maintenance windows are used in Opsflw day-2 operations to keep change rollout predictable and auditable.

docs.title: Why maintenance windows are used
docs.text:
• Reduce operational risk during upgrades and patching.
  • Coordinate monitoring and rollback readiness across platform components.
  • Keep service-impact communication consistent for customers.

docs.title: What users should do
docs.text:
1. Review the maintenance notice and expected impact.
  2. Avoid high-risk production changes during the window.
  3. Validate your critical workflows after completion.
  4. Report any regression through the support portal.

For urgent incidents during or after a maintenance window, submit a ticket with the highest appropriate severity and include clear business impact.

docs.title: Troubleshooting access issues
docs.text:
Users occasionally lose access to Opsflw Connect services after role changes or network adjustments. Follow the collapsible checks below to restore access while maintaining security controls.

Validate account status

Confirm the user exists in the identity provider and is mapped to the correct Opsflw Connect role.

opsflowctl iam user get --email user@example.com

If the account shows as suspended, reinstate the user in the identity provider and re-run the command to confirm the change propagated.

Review recent role assignments

Audit the permissions granted to the user to ensure they cover the requested resource. Compare the existing role with the entitlement matrix in the platform runbook.

opsflowctl iam role assignment list --user user@example.com

When a role is missing, reapply the mapping and document the adjustment in the change management system.

Check for network restrictions

Access issues can also stem from network policy updates. Validate that the user's source IP range is still allowed through the relevant firewall rules or VPN configuration. Coordinate with the networking team if changes are required.

docs.title: Troubleshooting build failures
docs.text:
Opsflw Connect documentation builds fail most often because a required preflight step was skipped or a recent content change broke navigation. Use the checks below to quickly restore a green pipeline.

Confirm required tooling

Verify that the global Python and Node dependencies match the repository requirements. Install or upgrade them with the project-provided manifests.

pip install --user -r requirements.txt
npm install

If the install commands report missing permissions, ensure you are not running inside a restricted container or shell session. Retry after enabling the recommended user-level package directories.

Run the preflight suite locally

Execute the same commands that CI uses before opening a pull request. Address any failures before re-running the suite.

mkdocs build --strict
npx markdownlint-cli "docs/**/*.md"
npx playwright test

Resolve navigation warnings from mkdocs build by checking mkdocs.yml for incorrect paths or duplicate headings. Fix lint errors by wrapping long lines or adding the required blank lines around fenced code blocks.

Capture failing output for review

When the build still fails, copy the command output into your pull request or support ticket. Include the exact command, the error snippet, and any recent content changes. This context helps reviewers reproduce the issue quickly.

docs.title: Troubleshooting formatting gallery
docs.text: Use this gallery as a reference when crafting troubleshooting runbooks with rich Markdown patterns.

docs.title: Quick reference table
docs.text: Pattern Use case Example snippet Callout Highlight critical action !!! warning Task list Track resolution steps - [ ] Restart service Code block Share command sequence ```bash

docs.title: Callouts and block quotes
docs.text:
Escalate for repeated failures

If the workflow fails more than three times in a row, open a Sev-2 incident. Page the on-call engineer immediately.

Tip: You can nest actionable notes within a quote to show the operator context before the task begins.

docs.title: Lists and checklists
docs.text:
• Primary steps
  • [x] Verify the incident ID
  • [ ] Capture relevant logs
  • [ ] Update the status page
  • Follow-up actions
  • File the post-incident report
  • Schedule a retrospective meeting
  • Share findings with stakeholders

docs.title: Code and configuration
docs.text:
kubectl logs deploy/opsflw-api --tail=200 | tee opsflw-api.log

alert_rules:
  - name: api-latency-spike
    threshold_ms: 450
    notify: platform-oncall

Inline code such as opsflowctl diagnose helps readers spot precise command names quickly.

docs.title: Tabs for platform variants
docs.text:
=== "Cloud" Run opsflowctl diagnose --profile cloud to gather managed service diagnostics.

=== "Self-hosted" Run opsflowctl diagnose --profile edge --include=metrics to include Prometheus snapshots.

docs.title: Definition list and footnote
docs.text:
API gateway | Fronts inbound requests and terminates TLS. Message bus | Buffers event traffic before delivery to processors.

Cite the incident source of truth in every runbook update.1

docs.title: Embedding media
docs.text: Use captions or context paragraphs so operators understand why the media matters.

docs.title: Task success criteria
docs.text:
1. Document the failure signature in the incident record.
  2. Confirm the impacted integration is re-enabled.
  3. Close the incident once platform health returns to green across all regions.

Following these patterns keeps troubleshooting content actionable and scannable.

  1. Link to the incident record in Opsflw Tracker. ↩

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: Use the Opsflow REST API to programmatically manage runs and pipelines. Authenticate with a bearer token generated in the Opsflow console.

docs.title: List Pipelines
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/pipelines
Authorization: Bearer <token>

Returns pipeline metadata including the latest revision.

docs.title: Trigger a Run
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/pipelines/{pipeline_id}/runs
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "parameters": {
    "region": "us-east-1",
    "priority": "high"
  }
}

Response contains the run ID you can poll via GET /api/v1/runs/{run_id}.
